newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Flat Australian dollar hampered by holidays.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Flat Australian dollar hampered by holidays.

text.p: The Australian dollar started 1997 on a subdued note, held to a narrow range as holidays in other centres hampered liquidity and interest, traders said.
The dollar traded a US$0.7940/46 range on the day after softening from above US$0.7960 in offshore trade on New Year's Eve, traders said, describing market conditions as dead.
That softer tone remained when the market reopened after Wednesday's New Year holiday, support holding at US$0.7940.
By 4.30 p.m. (0530 GMT) the Australian dollar was almost motionless at US$0.7941/46, level with an early US$0.7942/52 and US$0.7966/71 at the local close on Tuesday.
Trade on Thursday remained thin, hampered by holidays in Japan, Singapore and New Zealand, and this explained the static nature of the local market on the day, traders said.
The story was much the same on the crosses. In trade weighted terms the dollar held steady through the day at 59.1 after dropping offshore from Tuesday's close of 59.4.

Against the yen, it ended at 91.96/06, almost level with its opening 92.00/10, but down on its 92.39/49 close to 1996. The stalling of the U.S. dollar near 116 yen kept the local unit trading just above 92 yen for most of the day, traders said.
The Tokyo market is closed again on Friday, and traders said there was little reason to expect the market would return to normal trading conditions until next week.

Next week also sees the first significant local data releases of the year, with the November current account deficit due on Monday, and retail trade and building approvals data for the same month on Tuesday.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics released their business expectations survey, but due to the timing of the release and the fact that it is a relatively new series, it had little market impact.
The series is only three years old, limiting any comparison and interpretation of the data, economists said.

The survey was also held during the December quarter, which economists said meant most responses would have been made by the time the third rate cut on December 11, taking official interest rates down to 6.0 percent, was announced.

"It is probably best, therefore, to regard these expectations as reflecting the state of the economy that led to the rate cuts, rather than an assessment of the economy after the cuts," Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton said.
